people.name: Dzmitry Bahdanau
people.famous_for: Additive attention for neural machine translation (2014)
people.text: Then a PhD student at Université de Montréal, Bahdanau added a learned alignment score to seq2seq translation — letting the decoder look back at encoder states, the direct ancestor of query–key attention.

people.name: Ashish Vaswani
people.famous_for: Lead author of 'Attention Is All You Need' (2017)
people.text: Google Brain researcher whose 2017 paper removed recurrence entirely and made self-attention the whole architecture — the transformer. Later co-founded Adept AI and Essential AI.

people.name: Geoffrey Hinton
people.famous_for: Popularising backpropagation; 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics
people.text: Co-author of the 1986 paper that made backpropagation famous and of AlexNet's lineage; Turing Award 2018. Left Google in 2023 to speak freely about AI risk.

people.name: Ilya Sutskever
people.famous_for: AlexNet co-author, seq2seq co-inventor, OpenAI co-founder
people.text: Helped open the deep-learning era (AlexNet 2012), co-invented the seq2seq model that attention was built to fix (2014), and drove GPT's scaling culture at OpenAI before co-founding Safe Superintelligence in 2024.

people.name: Noam Shazeer
people.famous_for: Transformer co-author; sparsely-gated mixture of experts (2017)
people.text: Prolific Google researcher behind MoE layers, Mesh-TensorFlow and much of the transformer codebase; co-founded Character.AI, then returned to Google in 2024.

people.name: Andrej Karpathy
people.famous_for: OpenAI co-founder, Tesla AI director, nanoGPT and the Zero-to-Hero lectures
people.text: Taught a generation of engineers how transformers actually work — his 'Let's build GPT' videos and nanoGPT made the internals public; also coined 'vibe coding'.

people.name: Tomas Mikolov
people.famous_for: word2vec (2013) — the first famous embedding space
people.text: Google researcher whose skip-gram model made 'king − man + woman ≈ queen' a headline — the first proof that geometry could hold meaning.

people.name: David Rumelhart
people.famous_for: Lead author of the 1986 Nature paper that popularized backpropagation
people.text: Psychologist-turned-connectionist whose 1986 Nature paper with Hinton and Williams made training deep nets practical — the single citation behind every gradient in this repo.

people.name: Frank Rosenblatt
people.famous_for: The perceptron (1958) — the first learning machine
people.text: Built the Mark I Perceptron as actual hardware — weights were motor-driven potentiometers. Minsky and Papert's 1969 critique of its limits helped trigger the first AI winter.

people.name: Jonathan Ho
people.famous_for: DDPM lead author (2020) and classifier-free guidance
people.text: Berkeley PhD student whose denoising-diffusion paper made score-based generation practical — and who then wrote the guidance trick every prompt box uses.

people.name: Paul Christiano
people.famous_for: Deep RL from human preferences (2017) — the original RLHF
people.text: Showed humans could train agents by ranking short clips instead of writing reward functions; led OpenAI's alignment team before founding the Alignment Research Center.

people.name: Tri Dao
people.famous_for: FlashAttention (2022) and the Mamba state-space line
people.text: His IO-aware rewrite of attention — compute the same numbers, never materialize the n×n matrix — became standard serving infrastructure; co-founded the SSM alternative.

people.name: Chris Olah
people.famous_for: Mechanistic interpretability; co-founder of Distill.pub and Anthropic's interp program
people.text: Turned 'feature visualisation' into a research field — circuits, superposition, monosemantic features — and now leads Anthropic's interpretability work.

people.name: Patrick Lewis
people.famous_for: Lead author of the RAG paper (2020)
people.text: Coined retrieval-augmented generation at Facebook AI for knowledge-intensive NLP; the pattern he named now underpins most enterprise LLM products.

people.name: Alec Radford
people.famous_for: GPT-1 and GPT-2 lead author; CLIP lead
people.text: Quiet author of much of the modern stack — the original generative pre-training papers, GPT-2's staged release, and the contrastive image-text model behind a decade of multimodal work.

people.name: Jason Wei
people.famous_for: Chain-of-thought prompting; the emergent-abilities study
people.text: Google Brain → OpenAI → Meta researcher who showed 'let's think step by step' unlocks reasoning, and catalogued abilities that seem to appear only at scale.

people.name: John Schulman
people.famous_for: PPO (2017); led ChatGPT's RLHF fine-tuning
people.text: Wrote the policy-gradient algorithm inside RLHF and ran ChatGPT's alignment training; later co-founded Thinking Machines Lab.

people.name: Diederik Kingma
people.famous_for: Adam (2014), the VAE (2013), flow matching (2022)
people.text: Authored both the optimizer almost every run uses and the variational/generative lineage that leads to modern flow matching.

people.name: Tero Karras
people.famous_for: StyleGAN family; the EDM diffusion framework
people.text: NVIDIA researcher whose progressive GANs dominated image generation pre-diffusion, then whose EDM paper cleaned up diffusion's design space and samplers.

people.name: Jared Kaplan
people.famous_for: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (2020); Anthropic co-founder
people.text: Physicist whose power-law fits at OpenAI turned 'just make it bigger' into a quantitative trade — then co-founded Anthropic.

people.name: Richard Sutton
people.famous_for: The RL textbook; 'The Bitter Lesson' (2019); Turing Award 2024
people.text: Wrote the standard text on reinforcement learning and its shortest manifesto: general methods that leverage compute beat hand-crafted knowledge.

people.name: Charles Goodhart
people.famous_for: Goodhart's law (1975)
people.text: Economist whose observation — a measure that becomes a target stops being a good measure — is the unofficial motto of ML evaluation and reward hacking.

theorems.name: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017)
theorems.text: Showed a stack of self-attention plus feed-forward layers — no recurrence, no convolution — beat the best translation models while training far more in parallel. The architecture became the transformer.

theorems.name: Universal approximation theorem
theorems.text: A feed-forward net with one hidden layer and a non-polynomial activation can approximate any continuous function on a compact set arbitrarily well (Cybenko 1989; Hornik 1991). Existence, not efficiency — depth is what makes it practical.

theorems.name: Chinchilla scaling law (Hoffmann et al., 2022)
theorems.text: DeepMind fit loss over 400+ training runs: compute-optimal training needs roughly 20 tokens per parameter — implying most large models of the era were undertrained, and smaller well-fed models beat them.

theorems.name: Self-attention is O(n²) in sequence length
theorems.text: QKᵀ computes every pair of tokens, so score memory and FLOPs grow quadratically with context length n. The whole long-context literature (FlashAttention, sliding windows, sparse and linear attention) is a workaround for this fact.

theorems.name: Kaplan scaling laws (2020)
theorems.text: Jared Kaplan's OpenAI team fit smooth power laws: test loss falls predictably as you scale parameters, data, or compute — and suggested bigger models were compute-efficient even if undertrained.
theorems.status: empirical fit; superseded in detail by Chinchilla

theorems.name: The Bitter Lesson (Sutton, 2019)
theorems.text: Seventy years of AI research says methods that leverage computation — search and learning — repeatedly beat methods built on human domain knowledge. Researchers keep learning this the hard way.

theorems.name: Double descent (Belkin et al., Nakkiran et al., 2019)
theorems.text: Test error can fall, then rise through the interpolation threshold, then fall again — 'bigger is better' only holds in the second regime, past the point where the model exactly fits the data.
theorems.status: empirical; proved for some model classes

theorems.name: Emergent abilities (Wei et al., 2022)
theorems.text: Capabilities that look absent in small models and suddenly present at scale — few-shot, arithmetic, instruction-following. Schaeffer et al. (2023) argued many are metric artefacts; whether emergence is real is still contested.

theorems.name: Goodhart's law
theorems.text: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure — the root pattern behind benchmark overfitting, reward hacking and metric games across ML.

theorems.name: Lost in the middle (Liu et al., 2023)
theorems.text: LLMs read their context U-shapedly: best recall for items at the start, decent at the end, worst in the middle — so where a retrieved document sits matters, not just whether it's there.
